seoTitle: Research Internships in Europe: Funded Routes for 2027
title: How to Find and Apply for Research Internships in Europe (2026-27)
content:
A European research internship is the cheapest research credential you can earn: a defined project inside a real group, a supervisor who can later write for you, and a line on the CV that reads as method experience rather than coursework. This guide covers where the positions live, what the flagship funded programmes actually pay in 2026-27, and how to apply so the application survives the first read.

The funded programmes worth knowing by name

DAAD RISE Germany is the best-documented route for undergraduates: it matches students from the US, Canada, the UK and Ireland with doctoral-research groups in biology, chemistry, physics, earth sciences, engineering and computer science, for a three-month summer placement. The scholarship pays €992 per month, adds health, accident and liability insurance, an international travel subsidy and a €160 travel stipend for the closing meeting. The 2026-27 window runs from 15 October to 30 November 2026 for summer 2027 placements, with references due by 15 December. Canadian applicants route through Mitacs, whose Globalink programme reserves up to 100 RISE positions.

Beyond RISE, three structures dominate. Erasmus+ traineeships fund enrolled students (and recent graduates, under national rules) for placements across Europe; the grant is set by each country's national agency, typically in the low hundreds of euros a month, and your home university's international office administers it. Summer research fellowships at ETH Zurich, EPFL, Cambridge and similar institutions run annual calls with stipends and accommodation support that vary by host — always read the host's own page. And EURAXESS lists paid research-assistant and pre-doctoral vacancies across Europe daily, including short contracts that behave like internships with salaries.

Where the positions actually live

Search in this order and you will find more than the general job boards show. First, EURAXESS and national portals (the German DAAD database, the Dutch AcademicTransfer, the Swedish varbi) — these carry the paid positions. Second, research-group pages directly: most groups list openings under 'Join' or 'Open positions', and small groups rarely cross-post. Third, the structured programmes above, whose deadlines are annual and predictable. Fourth, your own professors' networks: a two-line email asking 'does your collaborator in Leiden need a summer student?' outperforms fifty cold applications.

What a placement costs the host, and why that matters to you

Groups host interns when the marginal cost is low and the marginal value is real. A funded programme like RISE pays you directly, so the host provides only supervision and a desk — easy to say yes to. An unfunded request asks the group for months of stipend money, which is why cold unfunded asks fail. The practical implication: apply through funded channels first, and if you approach a group directly, mention the funding you bring (Erasmus+ grant, scholarship, home-university bursary) in the first paragraph. Supervisors say yes to financed students.

[[chart:ask-success]]

The application that survives the first read

Internship applications are read in under two minutes, so structure for that reader. One page: a CV with one detailed research entry (question, method, your role, outcome), a three-paragraph letter naming the group's actual work and one skill you bring, and a transcript. Tailor the first sentence of the letter per group — the CV and transcript stay identical. Apply to eight to twelve placements rather than three, stagger across deadlines, and track everything in one sheet. References: one professor is enough for most programmes; brief them with the same four-week schedule you would use for degree applications.

Turning the internship into the next step

An internship compounds if you treat it as a two-way audition. Agree on a concrete deliverable in week one — a working pipeline, a validated dataset, a drafted section — and review it with your mentor at the midpoint. Ask for the reference conversation in the final week, while your work is fresh, and ask specifically: 'would you be comfortable writing that you did X with method Y to result Z?' Keep the code or notes you can ethically keep, and write your own summary before you leave; six months later it becomes the evidence paragraph of your master's or PhD application. Many funded placements end with exactly the supervisor relationship that funded doctorates are built on — UKRI studentships pay £21,805 in 2026/27, and the strongest applicants arrive already knowing how a group works.

The table is also a time-allocation guide. Structured programmes have fixed windows and fixed money, so they absorb most applications; direct asks are unlimited but succeed only when you bring funding, so they should carry the funding sentence in their first paragraph. Paid vacancies move fastest — contract roles are filled within days of posting — which makes a daily EURAXESS alert the single highest-yield subscription in this whole process.

The money and the maths of a European internship

Work the numbers before you accept anything. The RISE package of €992 a month for three months plus insurance covers a German university town comfortably — against the 2026 blocked-account release of €992, the stipend matches the official student living standard by design. Erasmus+ grants at €300-500 a month rarely cover full costs, so budget a personal contribution of €300-600 for a two-month placement, and check whether the host offers subsidised accommodation, which is often worth more than a stipend top-up. Paid vacancies on EURAXESS behave like junior salaries and are the strongest financial option when they appear. Travel and visa costs are the last line: Schengen short-stay visas cost €80 with processing of two to three weeks, and non-EU students on UK programmes should check whether their CAS-free short course needs a Standard Visitor visa instead.

Insurance is the item applicants forget until it bites. Funded programmes include health cover — RISE explicitly provides health, accident and liability insurance — but direct, unfunded placements leave it to you: a month of European travel insurance is cheap, a hospital visit without it is not. Erasmus+ requires a learning agreement signed by home university, host and you before departure; that document also unlocks the grant, so start it the week the placement is confirmed.

[[chart:intern-budget]]

Visas and logistics for short research stays

Short stays have simple but strict rules. Non-EU nationals entering the Schengen area for up to 90 days in any 180 use a short-stay visa (or visa-free access where an ETIAS authorisation applies once operational); the invitation letter from the host — stating dates, purpose and funding — is the document that makes the application routine, so request it the day your placement is confirmed. The UK is separate: research placements of up to six months can sit under the Standard Visitor visa route for unpaid academic activity, while paid placements need the correct work permission — interns on funded programmes receive the paperwork from the host, and anyone paid directly by a UK institution should confirm the route with its HR before booking travel. Canada’s Mitacs Globalink handles paperwork for its successful RISE candidates centrally.

Timing ties the logistics together: invitation letter in week one, visa application in week two, accommodation application the same fortnight — European summer housing in university towns is booked by March. Keep every confirmation as a single PDF pack; border officers and university admins both move faster when the story is one document long.

[[chart:visa-timeline]]

Questions applicants often ask

How much does a research internship in Europe pay?

Funded programmes pay real money: DAAD RISE pays €992 a month for three months plus insurance and travel support, Erasmus+ traineeship grants typically run in the low hundreds of euros a month (set by national agencies), and institutional summer fellowships vary by host. Paid pre-doctoral vacancies listed on EURAXESS pay local junior salaries.

When should I apply for summer research internships?

Autumn. RISE Germany opens 15 October and closes 30 November 2026 for summer 2027, with references due 15 December. Most European summer fellowships and Erasmus+ nominations sit between October and February. Start shortlisting groups in September.

Can I get a research internship without prior research experience?

Yes — that is what the structured programmes are for. They select on grades, coursework in the field and a credible letter; what they need is evidence you can learn a method, not that you already have publications. One detailed coursework project honestly described beats an inflated CV.

Official sources and further reading

Programme rules and amounts change every cycle; confirm on the official pages before applying.
